svg.title: VLAN, VRF, zone and SGT are four different concepts; what each one isolates, and why a VRF is not a security domain
svg.desc: Top: four concepts in one table. A VLAN or subnet partitions the Layer 2 broadcast domain and gives basic isolation that still needs Layer 3 policy as a supplement. A VRF partitions the routing table and allows overlapping address spaces; with no inter-VRF routing there is no connectivity at all, which makes it strong isolation by absence of a path - but it performs no inspection and produces no log of what it blocked. A firewall zone is a stateful policy boundary, so it isolates with inspection capability. An SGT is an identity tag that authorises independently of addresses. Middle left: the same subnet 10.0.0.0/24 exists inside two VRFs - the red and blue tenants - each router keeping its own table, so the duplicate address is not a conflict because the two worlds never meet. The only way from one to the other is an explicit route leak through a firewall, which is the point where a policy and a log appear. Middle right: three common confusions - treating a VRF as a security domain because it isolates, forgetting that a route leak turns isolation into a silent hole, and assuming a zone exists because a subnet exists. Bottom: the mapping to keep straight - VRF answers where an address space lives, a zone answers what policy applies, an SGT answers who the user is, and only the zone and the SGT produce evidence.
svg.text: VRF, VLAN, zone and SGT are not synonyms for "segment"
Each one answers a different question, and only two of the four can tell you afterwards what they blocked
CONCEPT
WHAT IT ISOLATES
STRENGTH AND WHAT IT IS NOT
VLAN / subnet
The Layer 2 broadcast domain
Basic isolation; still needs a Layer 3 policy above it. Not a policy at all - it only decides who can hear whom.
VRF
The routing table - address spaces may overlap
Strong isolation by absence of a path. Not inspection: it blocks by having no route, so there is nothing to log.
Zone (firewall)
The policy boundary, with session state
Isolation with inspection, logging and visibility. Not an address construct - a zone can contain many subnets.
SGT
Nothing - it labels identity
Authorisation independent of address. Not inspection either: a compromised host keeps its tag and its permissions.
THE SAME SUBNET IN TWO WORLDS
VRF RED
own routing table
own default route
no neighbour sees it
VRF BLUE
identical addresses,
no conflict - because
the tables never meet
the only bridge:
route leak
through a firewall
THREE CONFUSIONS THAT COST REAL MONEY
1 · "The VRFs are separate, so it is segmented."
True until someone adds a route leak for a project. Now two tenants
share a path, and no log records the decision.
2 · "A route leak is just one line."
It is a permanent policy decision with no expiry and no audit trail.
3 · "There is a subnet, so there is a zone."
Keep the mapping straight:
VRF = where the address space lives · zone = what policy applies · SGT = who the user is. Only the zone and the SGT
produce evidence afterwards; a VRF that blocks by having no route leaves you with nothing to show an auditor.
Design note: write the VRF-to-zone table into the design document. Nine times out of ten the argument in an incident is not about the policy but about which of these four concepts somebody assumed.
